CRIMINAL TRADE SECRET THEFT — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme Corp.

PURPOSE OF THIS CRIMINAL TRADE SECRET THEFT INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California Penal Code section 499c, the state's criminal trade secret theft statute -- what conduct it defines as a crime, how it defines "trade secret" for that purpose, and the penalties it specifies. It is prepared by Jane Doe concerning a situation involving Acme Corp. and, where relevant, John Smith. The trade secret information at issue is described as follows: customer pricing formulas. This Information Sheet is a general informational reference describing what section 499c says. Section 499c is a criminal statute: violations are prosecuted by public prosecutors (a district attorney or the Attorney General), not through a private lawsuit, and this document does not initiate, threaten, or request any criminal prosecution or investigation. It does not state that any specific conduct described above does or does not violate section 499c, and it is not a substitute for that case-specific legal determination. This document is also distinct from, and does not replace, this project's existing Trade Secret Misappropriation Cease and Desist Letter and Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet documents, both of which concern California's separate civil Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA) framework.

PENAL CODE SECTION 499C'S DEFINITION OF "TRADE SECRET"
Penal Code section 499c defines "trade secret," for purposes of this criminal statute, as information -- including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process -- that derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use, and that is the subject of efforts reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy. This definition is a separate statutory definition, stated within section 499c itself for criminal-law purposes, from the civil definition of "trade secret" in California's Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA), Civil Code section 3426.1, subdivision (d). As fetched and compared side by side, the operative wording of the two definitions is the same, differing only in that section 499c labels its two conditions (A) and (B) where CUTSA labels the same two conditions (1) and (2).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(9) “Trade secret” means information, including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process, that: (A) Derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use; and (B) Is the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 499c(a)(9) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California's criminal trade secret theft statute, definition of "trade secret" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=499c.)
  "(d) “Trade secret” means information, including a formula, pattern, compilation, program, device, method, technique, or process, that: (1) Derives independent economic value, actual or potential, from not being generally known to the public or to other persons who can obtain economic value from its disclosure or use; and (2) Is the subject of efforts that are reasonable under the circumstances to maintain its secrecy."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, definition of "trade secret" (quoted here for direct comparison to Penal Code section 499c's definition) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.1.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes Cal. Penal Code § 499c(a)(9), one subdivision (subparagraph (9) of subdivision (a)) of a single statutory section; it does not restate the other eight definitions in subdivision (a) ("access," "article," "benefit," "computer system," "computer network," "computer program," "copy," and "representing"), which are not otherwise addressed in this document. The observation that this definition's wording matches Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(d)'s CUTSA definition is this researcher's own side-by-side textual comparison of the two statutes as fetched from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, not a holding from any case that has compared them, and no case law testing that comparison is included here. That the wording matches does not mean the two statutes necessarily apply identically in every case: section 499c is a criminal statute construed by criminal courts and, where applicable, the standard of proof and rules of construction applicable to penal statutes, while Civil Code section 3426.1 is a civil statute; this document does not address whether or how those differences could affect how the same wording is applied in a criminal case versus a civil case. Both Cal. Penal Code § 499c and Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1 were each retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as separate HTTP requests using two different User-Agent headers; the statutory-text portion of each pair of retrievals was byte-identical (the only differences between the two retrievals of the same page were session-specific timestamp/ID strings embedded in unrelated page JavaScript, not the statutory text itself).

PROHIBITED ACTS: THEFT OF A TRADE SECRET UNDER SUBDIVISION (B)
Penal Code section 499c, subdivision (b), states that a person is guilty of theft if, with intent to deprive or withhold control of a trade secret from its owner, or intent to appropriate a trade secret to their own use or another's use, that person does any of four things: (1) steals, takes, carries away, or uses a trade secret without authorization; (2) fraudulently appropriates any article representing a trade secret entrusted to them; (3) having unlawfully obtained access to the article, without authority makes or causes to be made a copy of any article representing a trade secret; or (4) having obtained access to the article through a relationship of trust and confidence, without authority and in breach of the obligations created by that relationship, makes or causes to be made a copy of the article directly from and in its presence. Subdivision (b) itself states that a person who does any of these things "is guilty of theft"; it does not, within subdivision (b), separately state a felony/misdemeanor classification or a specific term of imprisonment or fine amount for this theft, unlike subdivision (c), addressed in a companion clause of this document, which does state its own specific penalty.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(b) Every person is guilty of theft who, with intent to deprive or withhold the control of a trade secret from its owner, or with an intent to appropriate a trade secret to his or her own use or to the use of another, does any of the following: (1) Steals, takes, carries away, or uses without authorization, a trade secret. (2) Fraudulently appropriates any article representing a trade secret entrusted to him or her. (3) Having unlawfully obtained access to the article, without authority makes or causes to be made a copy of any article representing a trade secret. (4) Having obtained access to the article through a relationship of trust and confidence, without authority and in breach of the obligations created by that relationship, makes or causes to be made, directly from and in the presence of the article, a copy of any article representing a trade secret."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 499c(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California's criminal trade secret theft statute, prohibited theft acts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=499c.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the full text of Cal. Penal Code § 499c(b), including its four numbered paragraphs (b)(1) through (b)(4); it does not quote subdivision (a) (the section's definitions, addressed in a companion clause), subdivision (c) (the bribery/inducement offense, addressed in a separate companion clause), or subdivision (d) (also addressed separately). This clause does not state what penalty applies to a violation of subdivision (b): because subdivision (b) states only that the described conduct "is guilty of theft" without itself specifying a punishment, this document does not independently trace or verify how California's general theft-classification statutes (which distinguish, among other things, grand theft from petty theft, generally based on the value involved) apply to a subdivision (b) violation, since those statutes were not fetched or verified as part of this research; a reader wanting that information would need to separately research those statutes. This clause does not state that any specific conduct does or does not fall within one of these four paragraphs.

PROHIBITED ACTS AND PENALTY: BRIBERY OR INDUCEMENT TO OBTAIN A TRADE SECRET UNDER SUBDIVISION (C)
Penal Code section 499c, subdivision (c), separately makes it a crime to promise, offer, give, or conspire to promise or offer to give a present or former agent, employee, or servant of another a benefit as an inducement, bribe, or reward for conveying, delivering, or otherwise making available an article representing a trade secret to a person not authorized by the owner to receive or acquire it. The same subdivision equally makes it a crime for a present or former agent, employee, or servant to solicit, accept, receive, or take such a benefit for doing the same thing. Unlike subdivision (b), subdivision (c) states its own specific penalty: imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or imprisonment under Penal Code section 1170, subdivision (h), or a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars, or both that fine and imprisonment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(c) Every person who promises, offers or gives, or conspires to promise or offer to give, to any present or former agent, employee or servant of another, a benefit as an inducement, bribe or reward for conveying, delivering or otherwise making available an article representing a trade secret owned by his or her present or former principal, employer or master, to any person not authorized by the owner to receive or acquire the trade secret and every present or former agent, employee, or servant, who solicits, accepts, receives or takes a benefit as an inducement, bribe or reward for conveying, delivering or otherwise making available an article representing a trade secret owned by his or her present or former principal, employer or master, to any person not authorized by the owner to receive or acquire the trade secret, shall be punished by imprisonment in a county jail not exceeding one year, or by imprisonment pursuant to subdivision (h) of Section 1170, or by a fine not exceeding five thousand dollars ($5,000), or by both that fine and imprisonment."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 499c(c) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California's criminal trade secret theft statute, bribery/inducement offense and penalty (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=499c.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the full text of Cal. Penal Code § 499c(c), including its stated penalty; it does not separately quote or explain Penal Code section 1170, subdivision (h) -- the realignment-era provision referenced within this penalty for the imprisonment option other than county jail -- which was not independently fetched or verified for this document. This clause does not restate subdivision (b) (the separate theft-type prohibited acts, addressed in a companion clause of this document) or subdivision (d) (also addressed separately). This clause does not state that any specific conduct does or does not fall within subdivision (c), and does not state that any specific penalty would or would not be imposed for any conduct.

RETURNING THE ARTICLE IS NOT A DEFENSE UNDER SUBDIVISION (D)
Penal Code section 499c, subdivision (d), states that in a prosecution for a violation of the section, it is no defense that the person returned, or intended to return, the article. By its own terms, this rule applies to a prosecution "for a violation of this section" generally -- it is not stated as limited to only subdivision (b) or only subdivision (c).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(d) In a prosecution for a violation of this section, it shall be no defense that the person returned or intended to return the article."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 499c(d) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California's criminal trade secret theft statute, return of article not a defense (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=499c.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes the entirety of Cal. Penal Code § 499c(d), a single one-sentence subdivision. It does not address any other defense that may or may not be available in a prosecution under this section, and no case law construing this subdivision was researched or is cited here.

RELATIONSHIP OF THIS CRIMINAL STATUTE TO CALIFORNIA'S CIVIL CUTSA FRAMEWORK
Penal Code section 499c is a criminal statute, enforced by public prosecutors, separate from California's civil Uniform Trade Secrets Act (CUTSA), Civil Code section 3426 et seq., which is enforced through private civil lawsuits. CUTSA's own non-supersession provision, Civil Code section 3426.7, states in subdivision (a) that CUTSA "does not supersede any statute relating to misappropriation of a trade secret, or any statute otherwise regulating trade secrets," and states in subdivision (b) that CUTSA "does not affect ... criminal remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret." As fetched, section 3426.7 does not name Penal Code section 499c, or any other specific criminal statute, by section number; it preserves "criminal remedies" and other trade-secret-related statutes only as a general category. This document does not go further than the statutory text to determine whether, or how, the two statutes' shared conduct requirements have been construed by courts.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Except as otherwise expressly provided, this title does not supersede any statute relating to misappropriation of a trade secret, or any statute otherwise regulating trade secrets. (b) This title does not affect (1) contractual remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret, (2) other civil remedies that are not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret, or (3) criminal remedies, whether or not based upon misappropriation of a trade secret."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7(a)-(b) (official leginfo.legislature.ca.gov text), California Uniform Trade Secrets Act, effect on other statutes and other remedies, including criminal remedies (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=3426.7.)
  Known gap: This clause cites Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.7, subdivisions (a) and (b) -- two subdivisions of one statutory section -- for the general proposition that CUTSA does not displace criminal remedies; it does not cite subdivision (c) of that same section (a public-records-specific carve-out addressed in a companion clause of this project's existing Trade Secret Preemption Doctrine Information Sheet document, not repeated here). The statement that section 3426.7 "does not name Penal Code section 499c ... by section number" is this researcher's own direct text search of the fetched statutory text of section 3426.7 for the string "499c," which did not appear; it is not a holding of any case. This clause does not identify or discuss any other statute that might also fall within CUTSA's general "any statute relating to misappropriation of a trade secret" language, and does not address whether a single set of underlying facts that supports a section 499c prosecution could also support a CUTSA civil claim, or how a criminal prosecution and a civil CUTSA claim arising from the same facts might interact procedurally (for example, as to timing, discovery, or use of one proceeding's evidence in the other) -- none of which is addressed by the statutory text quoted here or elsewhere researched for this document. Code § 3426.7 was retrieved twice directly from leginfo.legislature.ca.gov as two separate HTTP requests using different User-Agent headers; both retrievals returned byte-identical statutory text.
